Vignette:
# Kahu's Silence

Kahu was forty-eight when he first sat in the therapist's office, his large frame folded into a chair too small for him, calloused hands gripping his thighs. He had come because his wife, Aroha, had finally told him she could not live like this anymore—not the silence itself, which she had learned to navigate, but the way he had begun to disappear from their own home. He worked roofing jobs across the city, often taking on double shifts, returning after dark to eat alone in the kitchen while she slept. When she touched him, he flinched. When she asked him to sit with her, he found reasons to check the garage, reorganize the shed, anything to keep moving. Six months ago he had stopped eating regular meals, subsisting instead on coffee and the occasional protein shake consumed standing up between jobs. Aroha had noticed his weight dropping, the way his wedding ring had begun to slip on his finger, and she had wept—not out of anger, but out of a grief she could not name, watching her husband of twenty-two years turn into someone she could reach but never quite touch.

The assault had happened four years prior, on a Friday night after a work gathering at a bar in Southside. Kahu had gone with his crew, men he trusted, and had accepted a drink from someone he thought was a friend. What followed was a fragmented horror—a bathroom stall, hands that were not his own, a voice saying things he had trained himself not to remember in full. He had walked out of that bar and driven home in a state of numb shock, showered until his skin was raw, and told no one. For the first two years he had almost convinced himself it was something that had happened to someone else, a story he had heard rather than lived. But the body remembers what the mind tries to forget.

The triggers had accumulated slowly, then all at once. A news segment about sexual assault survivors would send him into a state of agitation that lasted hours—he had begun avoiding news entirely, asking Aroha to turn off the television, scrolling past headlines on his phone with a practiced flick of the wrist. Motorcycle noise, which had once been merely annoying, had become intolerable; the sound would arrest him mid-breath, his nervous system flooded with a sensation of being trapped, though he could not explain why the roar of an engine connected to that night. And alcohol—the smell of it, anywhere, in anyone's breath or on their clothes—would make his stomach turn, would send him back to that bathroom stall with a vividness that obliterated the present moment. He had stopped going to social events entirely.

What frightened him most was not the memories themselves, though those were terrible enough, but the way they no longer felt like memories at all. When he recalled the assault, it did not feel like something that had happened in the past; it felt as though it were happening now, with a clarity and immediacy that made his ordinary memories—his daughter's high school graduation, his mother's funeral, his wedding day—seem pale and distant by comparison. Sometimes, without warning, he would be standing on a roofline in the afternoon sun and would suddenly feel the full crushing weight of that night's terror, all the emotion and none of the image, as if his body knew something his mind was refusing to articulate. These moments would leave him hollow for hours afterward, and he would compensate by pushing harder, working longer, keeping his body moving so that his mind could not catch up.

The eating restriction had begun as a way to feel control—if he could govern what went into his body, perhaps he could govern what happened to it. But it had become its own kind of trap, and Aroha's worry had only made him more rigid, more determined to prove that he was fine, that nothing had changed, that he was still the man she had married. He was not fine. He was terrified that if he stopped moving, if he sat still long enough to feel the full weight of what had been taken from him, he would not be able to get back up. And he was afraid that Aroha would eventually leave, that his silence and his absence would wear through the bonds of their marriage until there was nothing left to hold onto. That fear, more than anything, was what had finally brought him to seek help—not hope that things could change, but desperation that they must.
